text:
[ScaleRec (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104318) directly matches multi-scale interest modeling: patches of different lengths, local Gaussian-biased attention for transient interests, inter-patch attention for sustained preferences, and context-adaptive aggregation. [HeteroTempRec (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2025.122703) combines local convolutions, global attention, personalized temporal fusion, and sparse historical-block selection. Both support explicitly separating temporal scales; their reported results do not establish gains under the pinned RecHarness evaluation.

[LSIDN (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14743) separates long-term session-interest evolution from short-term intent, with different denoising strategies for each. This suggests that indiscriminately pooling older interactions can mix incompatible interests. [BSARec (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28747) provides complementary motivation: self-attention can oversmooth representations; combining low- and high-frequency information preserves stable preferences and abrupt changes. Frequency components are modeling proxies, however, rather than observed intent labels.

Practical synthesis, proposed rather than established by these papers: retain SASRec and add prefix-only pooled item embeddings over several recent windows plus the full available prefix; learn a small gate conditioned on the current SASRec state to mix scales. Compare unchanged SASRec, one fixed window, multiple windows with fixed averaging, and adaptive gating under identical training settings and macro validation HR@10. A timestamp-gap or embedding-discontinuity gate could test changing intent without repeated item-pair edges. Searches found stronger direct support for multi-scale/session modeling than explicit change-point detection. Every pooling window, gate input, and session boundary must use only the prediction prefix; causal masking in SASRec alone does not guarantee auxiliary branches avoid future leakage.
